title: Boss: the 3 a.m. log hunt
summary: Answer real incident questions from an nginx access log, the way grep, cut, sort, uniq and sed would.

steps.title: The pager went off
body: The site is slow. You have `access.log` in nginx's common format, one request per line, fields separated by single spaces:
Note the quotes stay attached: field 5 is `"GET`, field 7 is `HTTP/1.1"`. Field 8 is the status, field 9 is the response size.
This time the log is real: your machine has it in `~/incident/access.log`, with `~/incident/nginx.conf` beside it.
Three terminals, three questions, the commands seniors type at 3 a.m.

steps.title: cut -d -f
prompt: Slice fields out of real files with `cut`:
1. `~/incident/ips.txt`: every client IP (field 1) in `~/incident/access.log`, each once, sorted.
2. `~/incident/bash-users.txt`: the login name (field 1 of `/etc/passwd`, fields split on `:`) of every account whose shell (field 7) is `/bin/bash`, in the file's order.

checks.name: ips.txt lists every client once, sorted
checks.fail: `~/incident/ips.txt` should be field 1 of every line, sorted, without duplicates.

checks.name: bash-users.txt names the bash accounts
checks.fail: `~/incident/bash-users.txt` should hold the login names of the accounts whose shell is `/bin/bash`, one per line.

hints: `cut -d' ' -f1 file` prints field 1 of each line; `sort -u` sorts and drops duplicates in one go.
First keep the right lines, then cut: `grep ':/bin/bash$' /etc/passwd | cut -d: -f1` (`$` anchors the end of the line).
steps.explain: `cut` is the scalpel for files with one clear separator: logs, CSVs, `/etc/passwd`. When the separator repeats (several spaces), reach for `awk '{print $1}'` instead.

steps.title: Who is hammering us?
prompt: Which clients get the most **server errors** (status 5xx, field 8)?
1. Write the top 3 to `~/incident/top-ips.txt` as `uniq -c` prints them (`count ip`), biggest first.
2. Write just the worst one's IP to `~/incident/block.txt` for the firewall team.

checks.name: top-ips.txt is the top 3 clients by 5xx count
checks.cmd: diff -w <(awk '$8 ~ /^5/' ~/incident/access.log | cut -d' ' -f1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -3) ~/incident/top-ips.txt
checks.fail: `~/incident/top-ips.txt` should be the three IPs with the most 5xx responses, each with its count, biggest first.

checks.name: block.txt holds the worst IP
checks.fail: `~/incident/block.txt` should hold just the IP at the top of your list.

hints: Keep only the 5xx lines first: `grep ' 5[0-9][0-9] ' access.log`, or `awk '$8 ~ /^5/'` (field 8 starts with 5).
Then the top N recipe on field 1: `| cut -d' ' -f1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -3`.
solution: awk '$8 ~ /^5/' access.log | cut -d' ' -f1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -3 > top-ips.txt
steps.explain: Filter, cut, count, rank: the same four moves answer "who" questions about any log. `awk '$8 ~ /^5/'` filters on one field, which is safer than a grep that could match a number anywhere on the line.

steps.title: sed s///
prompt: Before you attach the log to the ticket, anonymise it. Then fix the config that made things worse.
1. `~/incident/access.anon.log`: a copy of `access.log` with **every** IPv4 address replaced by `x.x.x.x`. Some request paths contain an address too. Leave `access.log` itself unchanged.
2. Edit `~/incident/nginx.conf` **in place** with `sed -i`: raise `worker_connections` from `512` to `4096`, and change the error log level from `debug` to `warn`. Change nothing else.

checks.name: access.anon.log has every address replaced
checks.fail: `~/incident/access.anon.log` should be `access.log` with every IPv4 address (also the ones inside paths) turned into `x.x.x.x`.

checks.name: access.log itself is unchanged
checks.fail: `access.log` was changed. Press Reset scenario: write the anonymised copy with `>` instead of editing in place.

checks.name: nginx.conf has the two fixes and nothing else
checks.fail: `~/incident/nginx.conf` should differ from the original in exactly those two lines.

hints: `sed -E` turns on extended regexes; an address is `[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+` (escape the dots). Without `g` only the first match on a line is replaced.
`sed -E 's/.../x.x.x.x/g' access.log > access.anon.log` writes a copy and leaves the original alone.
`sed -i 's/worker_connections 512;/worker_connections 4096;/' nginx.conf` edits in place; a second `-e 's/...'` (or a second command) handles the log level.
steps.explain: `sed -i` is how config changes are made on servers without an editor, in scripts and in Dockerfiles. Run it without `-i` first to see the result, then add `-i` (or `-i.bak` to keep a backup).
